Abstract
Recent studies show that using potential out-of-distribution
(OOD) labels from large corpora as auxiliary informa-
tion can improve OOD detection in vision-language mod-
els (VLMs). However, these methods often fail when real-
world OOD samples fall outside the predefined OOD la-
bel set. To address this limitation, we propose DynProto,
a novel approach that learns OOD prototypes dynamically
during testing using only in-distribution (ID) information.
DynProto is inspired by a key observation: OOD samples
predicted as the same ID class tend to cluster in the feature
space. With this insight, we leverage easy-to-detect OOD
samples as “anchors” to find their harder-to-detect, similar
counterparts. To this end, DynProto introduces two mod-
ules: Coarse OOD Pattern Capturing Module caches OOD
patterns that are easily confused with each ID class during
testing, and Fine-grained OOD Pattern Refinement Mod-
ule subsequently clusters these patterns within each cache
and aggregates them into representative OOD prototypes.
By measuring similarity to ID and dynamic OOD proto-
types, DynProto enables accurate OOD detection. Dyn-
Proto significantly outperforms prior methods across multi-
ple benchmarks. On ImageNet OOD benchmark, DynProto
reduces FPR95 by 11.60% and improves AUROC by 4.70%.
Moreover, the framework is architecture-agnostic and can
be integrated into various backbones.

Recent studies [5, 12, 19] have explored leveraging ex-
ternal corpora or large language models to generate candi-
date OOD labels. These methods treat the text embeddings
of constructed labels as potential OOD prototypes and pre-
dict test samples that are similar to these prototypes as OOD
class, achieving promising detection performance. How-
ever, since their effectiveness heavily depends on the qual-
ity of the constructed OOD prototypes, when OOD samples
encountered during testing go beyond the coverage of these
predefined labels, the effectiveness of such methods deteri-
orates significantly. Moreover, some of these methods care-
fully design potential OOD labels tailored to a specific ID
dataset and once the ID dataset changes, substantial effort
is required to redesign the labels.
To address these issues, we propose DynProto, a dy-
namic OOD prototype learning framework that generates
potential OOD prototypes only using ID-related informa-
tion to dynamically capture real OOD feature distributions.

The key idea originates from an interesting observation: we
found that some OOD samples predicted as the same ID
class share highly similar visual features, forming compact
clusters in the feature space. Although these OOD sam-
ples are similar, the model can only correctly detect part of
them, while the rest are still predicted as ID samples with
high confidence, leading to severe misclassification issues.
Based on this observation, we aim to dynamically col-
lect easily identifiable OOD samples during testing and use
them to generate OOD prototypes that attract other hard-to-
detect but similar OOD samples. To this end, we design
two modules: the Coarse OOD Pattern Capturing Module,
which maintains a per-class cache to dynamically collect
potential OOD visual features predicted as that class with
low confidence during testing, and the Fine-grained OOD
Pattern Refinement Module, which clusters cached samples
and aggregates features within each cluster into an OOD
prototype for fine-grained OOD pattern representation. In
addition, we construct ID prototypes from the training data.
The final decision for a test sample is based on the similarity
between the visual features of the test sample and the ID and
OOD prototypes. As shown in Figure 1, compared to meth-
ods that rely on external textual information, DynProto can
accurately capture the true OOD distribution during testing.
DynProto offers several distinct advantages. It does not
rely on any external prior information and requires no addi-
tional model training. Moreover, methods based on external
textual labels are limited to VLMs, whereas our method is
architecture-agnostic—it can be applied to both unimodal
and multimodal architectures. Furthermore, DynProto can
be built upon various OOD detection baselines, leveraging
them as base detectors. The stronger the base detector, the
higher the quality of the generated OOD prototypes. Our
main contributions can be summarized as follows:
• We reveal a key phenomenon that some OOD samples
predicted as the same ID class share similar visual fea-
tures, forming clusters in the feature space. Based on this,
we propose to use easily detected OOD samples as an-
chors to attract similar and hard-to-detect OOD samples.
• We propose DynProto, a training-free, architecture-
agnostic framework that dynamically learns OOD proto-
types during inference.
• Extensive experiments demonstrate that DynProto consis-
tently outperforms SOTA methods, reducing FPR95 by
11.60% and improving AUROC by 4.70% on the Ima-
geNet OOD benchmark with CLIP-B/16.
2. Related Work
Prototype Learning.
A prototype is a representative
feature embedding of a class, used to compute similar-
ity between test features and the prototype for classifica-
tion or representation learning.
Recently, many studies
have introduced prototype learning into OOD detection.
SIREN [11] shapes hyperspherical feature representations
with von Mises–Fisher prototypes to enhance separabil-
ity between ID and OOD samples. CIDER [32] improves
OOD detection by enforcing compact intra-class and dis-
persed inter-class hyperspherical embeddings around learn-
able class prototypes. PALM [27] models each class with a
mixture of prototypes to better capture intra-class diversity.
DHE [57] uses hyperspherical embeddings to ensure prov-
able discrimination between ID and OOD samples by opti-
mizing class prototypes on the sphere. SPROD [56] refines
ID prototypes to mitigate the impact of spurious correla-
tions. While these methods improve OOD performance by
learning more representative ID prototypes, little attention
has been paid to capture meaningful representations of true
OOD samples. While POP [14] learns virtual OOD pro-
totypes to reshape the decision boundary between ID and
OOD data, these prototypes can not accurately capture the
distribution of true OOD data. Our method fully leverages
OOD data observed during testing, using them as anchors
to capture other OOD patterns with similar characteristics.
OOD Detection Based on External Textual Information.
Benefiting from CLIP’s [37] strong generalization capa-
bility in open-world scenarios, many recent methods have
leveraged its rich textual knowledge by obtaining potential
OOD text labels from external text corpora or large lan-
guage models to assist CLIP in OOD detection. ZOC [12]
trains a captioner on external datasets to generate potential
OOD text labels. NegLabel [19] incorporates the Word-
Net [29] to mine semantically unrelated words to the ID
labels. CSP [5] enhances the activation probability of labels
by constructing a set of low-correlation super-class labels.
NegRefine [2] refines negative-label-based zero-shot OOD
detection by filtering semantically ambiguous labels and in-
troducing a multi-matching-aware scoring strategy. Syn-
OOD [21] employs a diffusion-based in-painting pipeline
to generate near-boundary OOD images, and then finetunes
the CLIP model by aligning those synthetic samples with
negative text-label features drawn from an external label
space beyond the ID classes.
Test-Time OOD Detection. Recently, growing attention
has been devoted to utilizing information from real test-
time scenarios to enhance OOD detection. AUTO [46] con-
ducts test-time adaptation by directly optimizing the model
via stochastic gradient descent, with the objective of reduc-
ing overconfidence on potential OOD samples. RTL++ [13]
models a linear relationship between OOD scores and fea-
tures, but this assumption fails when the feature spaces of
near OOD and ID samples overlap. AdaND [4] keeps the
backbone model fixed and trains a lightweight noise detec-
tor to identify and filter out OOD samples. TULIP [52] in-
corporates prior knowledge of ID and OOD distributions
during test time to calibrate the model’s predictive uncer-
tainty.

AdaNeg [51] constructs a memory bank for each predefined

3.2. Overview
As shown in Figure 2, we propose DynProto, a dynamic
prototype learning framework for OOD detection. Unlike
existing methods that rely on pre-defined textual OOD pro-
totypes, DynProto constructs class-aware visual OOD pro-
totypes dynamically during testing, only using ID-related
information. We design two modules. The Coarse OOD
Pattern Capturing Module (COPC, Section 3.3) maintains
a class-wise cache to collect test samples predicted as each
ID class with low OOD scores, and the Fine-grained OOD
Pattern Refinement Module (FOPR, Section 3.4) performs
clustering on the cached samples and aggregates the fea-
tures within each cluster to form an OOD prototype, en-
abling fine-grained representation of OOD patterns. After
that, we use DynProto score (Eq. 4) to determine whether a
sample belongs to the ID. Finally, we discuss the cold start
strategy of DynProto (Section 3.5). During the cold start
phase, when the caches contain only a few samples, Dyn-
Proto relies on a base OOD detector for sample collection.
As testing proceeds and more diverse samples are collected,
we use DynProto score for sample collection.

3.3. Coarse OOD Pattern Capturing
To construct OOD prototypes, we first need to collect di-
verse OOD patterns. We maintain a cache for each ID class,
which is initially empty. Given an input x, we feed it into
detector and get an OOD score. If the score of x is lower, it
is more likely to be an OOD sample. Therefore, if the score
of x is lower than a predefined threshold, x is regarded as a
potential OOD sample and its feature is stored in the cache
associated with the predicted ID class.
To maintain efficiency, each cache is assigned a fixed ca-
pacity and updated using a first-in-first-out (FIFO) strategy.
When the cache is not full, the visual feature v of an OOD
candidate is directly stored in the cache of its predicted
class. If the cache is full, the oldest entry is removed be-
fore adding the new one. Based on temporal locality, recent
samples are more likely to be correlated with the current
test sample. Therefore, the FIFO strategy helps retain sam-
ples most relevant to the current testing environment while
discarding outdated ones, enhancing cache efficiency.
3.4. Fine-grained OOD Pattern Refinement
After cache updating, we use the collected samples to con-
struct OOD prototypes. For any non-empty cache, we per-
form BIRCH clustering [50] on the stored image features
to identify different OOD patterns associated with the same
ID class. Samples within the same cluster are aggregated
by averaging to form a single OOD prototype. Similarly,
ID training samples are aggregated by class to obtain one
ID prototype per class. We denote the prototypes as P =
[p1, p2, ..., pC, pC+1, ..., pC+M], where p1, ..., pC are ID
prototypes, and pC+1, ..., pC+M are constructed OOD pro-
totypes. C is the number of ID classes, and M is the number
of constructed OOD prototypes.
Given a test image feature v = F(x) ∈RD, we use
the NegLabel score (Eq. 3) to measure whether the sample

3.5. Cold Start
During the first Tcold iterations of testing, when the caches
contain only a few samples, we use the MSP score [17]
as the base OOD detector for unimodal models, while for
VLMs we adopt the MCM score [30] to determine which
test samples should be cached. We also experiment with
other methods as base detectors, and detailed analyses are
provided in Section 4.2. The score threshold for sample col-
lection is denoted by θ. Since the score distribution of OOD
samples is unavailable at test time, θ is estimated as the β-
th percentile of the OOD score distribution derived from ID
training data, with β = 5 in our experiments.
As testing proceeds and more samples are accumulated,
we stop using base detector and instead use DynProto
score for selecting potential OOD samples, as DynProto
score begins to outperform the base detector. Inspired by
OWTTT [22], a dynamic threshold α is introduced to enable
the model to adapt to varying sample distributions across
different batches. As reported in OWTTT, the OOD scores
exhibit a bimodal distribution, and the adaptive threshold is
obtained by minimizing intra-class variance. Accordingly,

4. Experiments
4.1. Experimental Setup
Datasets. We perform extensive experiments using both
the CIFAR-100 [20] and ImageNet [8] the as ID datasets.
In line with prior work [23, 30], we select SVHN [35],
LSUN-R [43], LSUN-C, iSUN [36], Texture [6], and
Places365 [54] as the OOD datasets for CIFAR-100. For
ImageNet, we use iNaturalist [40], SUN [44], Places [54],
and Textures [6] as far-OOD datasets, while NINCO [3] and
SSB-hard [41] are used as near-OOD datasets. We also ver-
ify the effectiveness of DynProto on three more ID datasets:
CIFAR10 [20], ImageNet100 [30], EuroSAT [16], and the
experimental results are provided in the Appendix B.
Implementation Details. We implement our method in Py-
Torch and conduct all experiments on a NVIDIA GeForce
RTX 3090 GPU with a batch size of 512. Following the
test-time adaptation protocol, we mix and randomly shuffle
ID and OOD samples. Each experiment is performed using
five distinct random seeds for shuffling. The cache size is
set to m = 30 for each class. The threshold θ is defined as
the β = 5th percentile of the OOD score distribution on the
ID training set. The cold-start period Tcold is set to 5, and
the coefficient K is set to 5.
Metric. We use two evaluation metrics: the false positve
rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) and the area under
the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).
Baselines. We adopt a comprehensive set of competitive
baselines for comparison. For Vision-Model-based OOD
detection, we follow standard practice and use DenseNet-
101 [18] and ResNet-50 [15] as backbones for CIFAR-
100 and ImageNet, respectively. The compared methods
include MSP [17], Energy [24], ReAct [39], DICE [38],
VIM [42], ASH-S [9], LINe [1], OptFs [53], OODD [47],
and CADRef [23].
For VLM-based OOD detection,
we use CLIP-B/16 as the backbone and compare against


MCM [30], CoOp [55], LoCoOp [34], NegLabel [19],
CSP [5], AdaNeg [51], AdaND [4], NegRefine [2], FA [28],
and SynOOD [21] as baselines.
Among them, OODD,
AdaNeg and AdaND are test-time adaptation methods. All
baselines are evaluated using their original hyperparameter
configurations to ensure fair comparison.

Impact of Cache Initialization.
Before testing begins,
we initialize the cache for each class as empty. Following
OODD [47], we further explore several alternative cache
initialization strategies and analyze their effects on the final
performance: (1) C-Out: randomly crop ID training sam-
ples and initialize the cache using cropped views with lower
OOD scores; (2) T-Out: randomly fill the cache with OOD
samples whose categories differ from the real OOD types;
(3) D-Out: initialize the cache using a subset of real OOD
samples. For each cache initialization strategy, we pre-store
the features of 800 samples into the cache before evalua-
tion. As shown in Table 4, the C-Out strategy yields the
worst performance. This is because, during the cropping
process, some ID-related information is inevitably stored
in the cache, leading to cache contamination. The T-Out
strategy achieves the best results, as initializing the cache
with real OOD samples effectively mitigates the transient
instability during the cold-start phase. However, in practical
testing scenarios, it is often infeasible to obtain real OOD
samples in advance, making this initialization strategy un-
realistic. The performance of D-Out is comparable to that
of initializing the cache as empty. Therefore, from a cost-
efficiency perspective, we initialize all caches as empty.

periments on ImageNet OOD benchmark to evaluate how
different hyperparameters influence the performance.
We first analyze the impact of the cache capacity m. A
larger cache consistently leads to better performance, as it
enables the cache to store more diverse OOD patterns.
Next, we investigate the effect of β, which determines
the OOD score threshold for sample collection during the
cold-start stage. In our experiments, β ranges from 0 to
100, and we evaluate values between 5 and 85. As illus-

which subsequently declines when the parameters continue
to grow. This trend can be explained as follows. When β
is small, only a limited number of OOD samples are ad-
mitted into the cache. As β increases, more OOD samples
are incorporated, improving the model’s ability to discrim-
inate between ID and OOD samples. However, once β ex-
ceed certain thresholds, the number of cached OOD sam-
ples reaches saturation, and additional increases cause more
ID samples to be mistakenly stored, leading to cache con-
tamination and a slightly drop in performance.

Many stud-

to the shortcut problem during training. When samples of a
certain ID class share similar backgrounds, the model tends
to use these background cues as decisive features for classi-
fication. Therefore, when OOD samples with similar back-
grounds but without the corresponding foreground objects
are fed into the model, it sometimes predicts them as that

6. Conclusion
We introduced DynProto, a test-time OOD detection frame-
work that dynamically constructs OOD prototypes during
inference, without requiring additional training or prede-
fined OOD labels. DynProto exploits the tendency of OOD
samples to cluster in the feature space. It uses easily de-
tectable OOD instances as anchors and identifies harder
cases through class-wise caching and clustering-based pro-
totype aggregation. Extensive experiments across a range
of OOD benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and ro-
bustness of our approach. The core idea behind DynProto
is general and could be extended to broader vision tasks,
which will be explored in future work.

A. Details of Datasets
A.1. ID Datasets
ImageNet [8] serves as one of the most widely used bench-
marks for large-scale image classification. It contains ap-
proximately 1.2 million training samples and 50,000 vali-
dation samples distributed over 1,000 semantic categories.
The dataset gathers images from a wide variety of natu-
ral scenes, encompassing diverse object domains such as
animals, plants, vehicles, and daily-use items. In our ex-
periments, we adopt the 50,000-image validation portion of
ImageNet-1K as the ID dataset.
CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 [20] are classic benchmark
datasets extensively used in computer vision and machine
learning research, both derived from the 80 Million Tiny
Images collection. CIFAR-10 contains 60,000 color images
of size 32 × 32, evenly distributed across 10 general object
categories—such as airplanes, cats, dogs, and trucks—with
6,000 images per category, including 50,000 for training
and 10,000 for testing. CIFAR-100, on the other hand, re-
fines this setup into 100 fine-grained categories organized
under 20 higher-level superclasses, while maintaining the
same total image count and resolution (500 training and 100
testing images per class).
A.2. OOD Dataset for Small-scale Dataset
In our experiments under the small-scale dataset setting,
we consider CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 as the ID datasets,
and use SVHN [35], LSUN-R, LSUN-C [43], iSUN [36],
Texture [6] and Places365 [54] as the corresponding OOD
datasets.
SVHN is a large-scale dataset derived from real-world
street imagery, where individual digit instances are cropped
from photographs of house numbers captured by Google
Street View. Unlike synthetic digit datasets, SVHN con-
tains complex visual variability, including diverse lighting
conditions, cluttered urban backgrounds, and irregular digit
placements, making it closer to natural image distributions.
In our experiments, the entire SVHN test set, consisting of
26,032 images, is utilized as an OOD dataset for perfor-
mance evaluation.
LSUN is a large-scale benchmark for scene classification,
encompassing a wide range of indoor and outdoor en-
vironments, including categories such as bedrooms, liv-
ing rooms, classrooms, and various building types. Two
commonly used variants, LSUN C and LSUN R, are con-
structed by applying random cropping and resizing transfor-
mations to the original LSUN images, respectively. In our
experiments, we sample 10000 images from each variant to
form the OOD datasets used for evaluation.
Places365 is a comprehensive large-scale dataset for scene
recognition, comprising images categorized into 365 dis-
tinct scene types that span a wide variety of indoor and out-
door environments. The official test set contains 900 sam-
ples per category. In this study, we construct an evaluation
subset by randomly sampling 100 images from each class,
resulting in a diverse and balanced collection used to assess
model performance across different scene contexts.
Textures is a dataset focused on recognizing material ap-
pearance and surface properties, containing 5640 texture
images categorized into 47 perceptually defined classes.
These classes represent diverse patterns and materials, such
as fabric, wood, and metal. Since there is no semantic over-
lap between the Texture dataset and CIFAR classes, we uti-
lize the entire dataset as OOD data in our experiments.
iSUN is a large-scale dataset developed for saliency and
visual attention research, containing 20608 natural scene
images originally sourced from the SUN database.
The
dataset includes human eye-tracking annotations, capturing
where people tend to focus when viewing complex real-
world scenes. 8925 images are selected from iSUN that
have no semantic overlap with the CIFAR dataset, using
them as OOD samples to evaluate model robustness on vi-
sually diverse and natural imagery.
A.3. OOD Dataset for Large-scale Dataset
In the large-scale dataset setting, we employ ImageNet as
the ID datasets. For OOD evaluation, we adopt iNatural-
ist [40], SUN [44], Places [54], and Textures as far-OOD
datasets, while NINCO [3] and SSB-hard [41] are used as
near-OOD datasets.
iNaturalist is a large-scale dataset of natural world im-
agery, encompassing 13 superclasses and 5,089 fine-grained
categories that span various biological domains such as
plants, insects, birds, and mammals. In this study, we utilize
a curated subset provided by MCM [30], which includes
110 plant categories carefully selected to ensure no seman-
tic overlap with ImageNet classes.
This subset contains
10000 images.
Places is a large-scale dataset of scene-centric images, cov-
ering a wide range of semantic environments categorized
into three broad domains: indoor, natural, and urban scenes.
For our experiments, we employ a subset curated by MCM,
which excludes any classes overlapping with ImageNet.
This curated subset contains 10000 images.
SUN is a comprehensive scene recognition dataset contain-
ing 397 well-defined categories commonly used for bench-
marking scene understanding models, and a total of 899


classes covering a wide range of indoor, urban, and natu-
ral environments, both with and without human presence.
In this study, we utilize a subset curated by MCM, which
removes any overlapping categories with ImageNet. The
resulting subset includes 10,000 images.
Textures is a dataset comprising 5640 images of textures
and abstract patterns, organized into 47 classes based on
human perceptual similarity. As none of its classes overlap
with ImageNet, the entire dataset was used as OOD dataset.
NINCO is a purpose-built dataset for OOD detection, de-
veloped to overcome the inherent limitations of ImageNet
benchmarks. It includes 64 OOD categories with a total
of 5879 images, each manually verified to ensure zero se-
mantic overlap with any ImageNet class. The images were
collected from a combination of existing datasets and newly
sourced web data, followed by meticulous cleaning to guar-
antee the complete absence of ID objects, making it a reli-
able benchmark for assessing OOD detection performance.
SSB-hard represents the most challenging split of the Se-
mantic Shift Benchmark (SSB), created to rigorously assess
OOD detection performance under subtle semantic varia-
tions. It contains 49000 images drawn from 980 ImageNet-
21K classes that were explicitly excluded from ImageNet.
These classes are both visually and semantically close to
the in-distribution categories, making SSB-hard a demand-
ing and reliable benchmark for evaluating hard-OOD detec-
tion scenarios.

D. More Analysis
D.1. Impact of Cache Update Strategies
In our current implementation, we adopt a FIFO policy for
cache updates, where the oldest entry is discarded once the
cache is full and a new OOD candidate is added. Further-
more, following OODD [47], we also evaluate an alterna-
tive strategy that replaces the cache entry with the highest
OOD score when inserting new samples (RH). Considering
that OOD types may exhibit abrupt changes in real-world
scenarios, we simulate a situation where different OOD
datasets appear sequentially over time. For instance, if the
order of OOD datasets is SUN →Places →Textures, it is
denoted as S →P →T. We simulate four such sequences:
S →P →T, T →S →P and P →S →T. Addi-
tionally, we also test a scenario where all OOD datasets are
mixed with the ID data and shuffled, denoted as “All”.
As shown in Table 15, our FIFO strategy consistently
outperforms the RH-based cache update strategy under dif-
ferent temporal drift scenarios, and also surpasses the base-
line method NegLabel [19] that relies on external textual
labels. According to the principle of temporal locality, the
current test sample is more likely to be correlated with its re-
cent samples. Therefore, adopting the FIFO strategy allows
the model to better capture the evolving OOD in real time.
In contrast, although the RH algorithm maintains a cache
containing many representative OOD patterns, as testing
progresses, the cache becomes dominated by earlier OOD
samples with relatively low scores that are rarely replaced.
Consequently, new OOD patterns fail to enter the cache,
leading to reduced cache circulation and degraded adapt-
ability to distributional drift. Moreover, in realistic OOD
detection scenarios, various OOD samples often appear in
a mixed and unpredictable manner. Even under such con-
ditions, our model consistently outperforms existing base-
lines. This demonstrates that our method can accurately
capture the dynamic evolution of OOD distributions, main-
taining strong robustness and adaptability in complex test-
ing environments.


D.2. Computation Cost.
DynProto introduces a modest computational overhead dur-
ing the caching and clustering stages, which we quantify
through empirical measurements. With CLIP-B/16 as the
backbone, standard CLIP inference runs at 453.29 FPS,
whereas our method reaches 428.67 FPS, accompanied by
an additional memory cost of 22 MB. Using ResNet-50
as the backbone, the standard inference speed is 841.43
FPS, while our approach achieves 811.90 FPS with an extra
memory overhead of 60 MB.
D.3. Limitations
As shown in Table 6, our method experiences performance
degradation when the number of ID samples significantly
outnumbers that OOD samples—although the incorpora-
tion of Gaussian noise effectively mitigates the extent of
this decline. Moreover, when encountering novel OOD data
types, our method experiences a slight performance dip in
the short term. As these new data types are cached, perfor-
mance rapidly rebounds.

Abstract: Recent studies show that using potential out-of-distribution (OOD) labels from large corpora as auxiliary informa- tion can improve OOD detection in vision-language mod- els (VLMs). However, these methods often fail when real- world OOD samples fall outside the predefined OOD la- bel set. To address this limitation, we propose DynProto, a novel approach that learns OOD prototypes dynamically during testing using only in-distribution (ID) information. DynProto is inspired by a key observation: OOD samples predicted as the same ID class tend to cluster in the feature space. With this insight, we leverage easy-to-detect OOD samples as “anchors” to find their harder-to-detect, similar counterparts. To this end, DynProto introduces two mod- ules: Coarse OOD Pattern Capturing Module caches OOD patterns that are easily confused with each ID class during testing, and Fine-grained OOD Pattern Refinement Mod- ule subsequently clusters these patterns within each cache and aggregates them into representative OOD prototypes. By measuring similarity to ID and dynamic OOD proto- types, DynProto enables accurate OOD detection. Dyn- Proto significantly outperforms prior methods across multi- ple benchmarks. On ImageNet OOD benchmark, DynProto reduces FPR95 by 11.60% and improves AUROC by 4.70%. Moreover, the framework is architecture-agnostic and can be integrated into various backbones.
